questions.questionText: Which one or more of the following options guarantee that a computer system will transition from user mode to kernel mode? Function Call malloc Call Page Fault System Call
questions.questionHtml:
Which one or more of the following options guarantee that a computer system will transition from user mode to kernel mode?

  1. Function Call
  2. malloc Call
  3. Page Fault
  4. System Call
questions.explanation: function call: functions may be user defined so It also does not guarantee to switch from user to kernel mode. Malloc () call : It can be done in both user and kernel modes. Hence, It cannot guarantee switching. Page fault : When a page fault occurs, required page must be loaded from secondary to main memory. It will be done in privileged mode and guarantee user mode to kernel mode switching. System call : System calls are executed  in kernel mode only. It definitely guarantee switching. Hence Ans is C,D. questions.questionHtml:

  1. The $\text{TLB}$ performs an associative search in parallel on all its valid entries using page number of incoming virtual address.
  2. If the virtual address of a word given by $\text{CPU}$ has a $\text{TLB}$ hit, but the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in the main memory.
  3. The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.

questions.explanation: Ans: Option C According to Galvin, “The TLB is associative, high-speed memory. Each entry in the TLB consists of two parts: a key (or tag) and a value. When the associative memory is presented with an item, the item is compared with all keys simultaneously. If the item is found, the corresponding value field is returned.” Hence option A is TRUE.    The TLB contains only a few of the page-table entries. If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit it means the the page number is found, so its frame number is immediately available and is used to access memory. Therefore even if the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, it does not matter. Its just not in cache memory but the word will always be present in the main memory as we already know the frame number due to the TLB Hit. Hence option B is also TRUE.    An Inverted Page Table has frame numbers as indexes unlike a Page Table where page number is used as index to it. There

Consider a computer system with multiple shared resource types, with one instance per resource type. Each instance can be owned by only one process at a time. Owning and freeing of resources are done by holding a global lock $(L)$. The following scheme is used to own a resource instance:

function OWNRESOURCE(Resource R)
    Acquire lock L // a global lock
    if R is available then
        Acquire R    
        Release lock L
    else
        if R is owned by another process P then     
        Terminate P, after releasing all resources owned by P    
        Acquire R    
        Restart P   
        Release lock L   
        end if   
    end if    
end function

  4. The scheme violates the mutual exclusion property

questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following pseudocode, where $\textsf{S}$ is a semaphore initialized to $5$ in line $\#2$ and $\textsf{counter}$ is a shared variable initialized to $0$ in line $\#1$. Assume that the increment operation in line $\#7$ is $\textit{not}$ atomic.

1.  int counter = 0;
2.  Semaphore S = init(5);
3.  void parop(void)
4.  {
5.         wait(S);
6.         wait(S);
7.         counter++;
8.         signal(S);
9.         signal(S);
10.  }

If five threads execute the function $\textsf{parop}$ concurrently, which of the following program behavior(s) is/are possible?

  1. The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $5$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$
  2. The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $1$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$
  3. The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $0$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$
  4. There is a deadlock involving all the threads

options.label: A
options.text: The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $5$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$

options.label: B
options.text: The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $1$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$

options.label: C
options.text: The value of $\textsf{counter}$ is $0$ after all the threads successfully complete the execution of $\textsf{parop}$

options.label: D
options.text: There is a deadlock involving all the threads

questions.questionHtml:
Let $M$ be a randomly chosen non-empty subset of $S=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 2026\}$.

Which of the following is the probability that the product of all the elements of $M$ is even?

  1. $2^{1013}\left(2^{1013}-1\right) / 2^{2026}$
  2. $2^{1013} / 2^{2026}$
  3. $2^{1013}\left(2^{1013}-1\right) /\left(2^{2026}-1\right)$
  4. $1 /\left(2^{2026}-1\right)$
questions.explanation: S = {1,2,3,....,2026} Total number of non-empty subsets of S: \[ 2^{2026} - 1 \] The product of elements of M is even if and only if M contains at least one even number. There are 2026 numbers in S. Number of even numbers = 1013   Number of odd numbers = 1013 The product is not even (i.e., odd) only if all selected elements are odd. Number of subsets formed only from odd numbers: \[ 2^{1013} - 1 \] Hence, number of subsets whose product is even: \[ (2^{2026} - 1) - (2^{1013} - 1) \] \[ = 2^{2026} - 2^{1013} \] \[ = 2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1) \] Therefore, required probability: \[ \frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1} \] Correct option: \[ {(C)} \]

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent random variables. $X$ follows $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p=0.3)$ distribution and $Y$ follows $\operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu=0, \sigma^{2}=100\right)$ distribution.

Which of the following options is the variance of $(2 X-1) Y$?

questions.explanation: Special Note: This question is taken from the exercise section of the textbook: A First Course In Probability by Sheldon M. Ross. \[ L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} \] The term \[ \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} \] is the PMF of a Poisson random variable with parameter $\lambda = n$. Hence, \[ \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} = P(X \le n), \quad X \sim \text{Poisson}(n). \] For large $n$, we use Central Limit Theorem(CLT) \[ X \sim \text{Poisson}(n) \] has \[ \mathbb{E}[X] = n, \quad \operatorname{Var}(X) = n. \] Thus, \[ X \approx N(n,n). \] Since we are standardizing the random variable $X$ itself, \[ Z = \frac{X - n}{\sqrt{n}}. \] (We divide by the standard deviation $\sqrt{n}$, not by $\sqrt{n}/\sqrt{n}$, because we are not dealing with a sample mean.) Therefore, \[ P(X \le n) = P\left( \frac{X-n}{\sqrt{n}} \le 0 \right). \] As $n \to \infty$, \[ \frac{X-n}{\sqrt{n}} \to N(0,1). \] Hence, \[ P(Z \le 0) = 0.5. \] \[ \boxed{L = 0.5} \] Correct Option: (A)

questions.questionText: A clinic specializes in testing for a disease $\text{D}$. The result of the test can be either positive or negative. A study revealed that if a person suffers from the disease $\text{D}$, the test result in that clinic comes out positive $80 \%$ of the time, and negative $20 \%$ of the time. If a person is not suffering from the disease $\text{D}$, the test comes out positive $10 \%$ of the time and negative $90 \%$ of the time. It is also known that among the general population, the disease $\text{D}$ occurs in $30 \%$ of the individuals. If a person tests positive for $\text{D}$ in that clinic, the probability that he/she actually suffers from the disease $\text{D}$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.questionHtml:
A clinic specializes in testing for a disease $\text{D}$. The result of the test can be either positive or negative.

A study revealed that if a person suffers from the disease $\text{D}$, the test result in that clinic comes out positive $80 \%$ of the time, and negative $20 \%$ of the time. If a person is not suffering from the disease $\text{D}$, the test comes out positive $10 \%$ of the time and negative $90 \%$ of the time. It is also known that among the general population, the disease $\text{D}$ occurs in $30 \%$ of the individuals.

If a person tests positive for $\text{D}$ in that clinic, the probability that he/she actually suffers from the disease $\text{D}$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Let D = person has disease $\bar{D}$ = person does not have disease + = test result is positive   Given: \[ P(D) = 0.30, \quad P(\bar D) = 0.70 \] \[ P(+|D) = 0.80 \] \[ P(+|\bar D) = 0.10 \] We need to compute: \[ P(D|+) \] Using Bayes’ theorem: \[ P(D|+) = \frac{P(+|D)P(D)} {P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|\bar D)P(\bar D)} \] Substituting values: \[ P(D|+) = \frac{0.80 \times 0.30} {0.80 \times 0.30 + 0.10 \times 0.70} \] \[ = \frac{0.24} {0.24 + 0.07} = \frac{0.24}{0.31} \] \[ = 0.77419 \] Rounded to two decimal places: \[ \boxed{0.77} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 24 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
For a given data set $\left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}$, where $n=100$, it is known that
\[
\frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}=99
\]
Let us denote $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}$

The value of $\frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Solution: Given: \[ n = 100 \] \[ \frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 99 \] We use the following important identity: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2n \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \] This identity relates the total pairwise squared differences to the total sum of squared deviations from the mean. It follows from expanding \[ (x_i - x_j)^2 = (x_i - \bar{x} - (x_j - \bar{x}))^2 \] and simplifying using \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0. \] Now apply the identity. Since \( n = 100 \), \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2(100) \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 200 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \] Substitute into the given equation: \[ \frac{1}{2000} \cdot 200 \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 99 \] \[ \frac{1}{10} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 99 \] \[ \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 990 \] Now compute the required value: \[ \frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \frac{990}{99} = 10 \] Final Answer: \[ \boxed{10} \] Aditya Jyotishi

\]
What is the probability that $n_i \ge 1$ for all $i \in \{1,2,3,4\}$?

  1. $\dfrac{\binom{19}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}}$

questions.explanation: We can choose $ n_i $ for $$ n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + n_4 = 20,\quad n_i \ge 0 $$ in $$ \binom{20 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{23}{3} $$ ways.  Now the requirement is $ n_i \ge 1 $. So write each variable as: $$ n_i = x_i + 1,\quad x_i \ge 0 $$ Substituting: $$ (x_1+1) + (x_2+1) + (x_3+1) + (x_4+1) = 20 $$ $$ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 + 4 = 20 $$ $$ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 16,\quad x_i \ge 0 $$ Number of solutions: $$ \binom{16 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{19}{3} $$ Therefore, $$ P = \frac{\binom{19}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}} $$ Devanshu_Gaur answered Feb 17 Devanshu_Gaur comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $$S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,2026\}$$A non-empty subset $M \subseteq S$ is chosen uniformly at random.

What is the probability that the product of all elements of $M$ is even?

  1. $\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$

     
  2. $\dfrac{2^{1013}}{2^{2026}}$

     
  3. $\dfrac{1}{2^{2026}-1}$

     
  4. $\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}}$
questions.explanation: 1. Probability of an even product Answer: A. $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$ The set $S$ has 2026 elements, 1013 of which are even and 1013 of which are odd. The total number of non-empty subsets of $S$ is $2^{2026} - 1$. The product of elements in a subset $M$ is even if and only if $M$ contains at least one even number. It is easier to calculate the probability of the complementary event: the product is odd. The product is odd if and only if all elements in $M$ are odd. The number of odd elements in $S$ is 1013. The number of non-empty subsets containing only odd elements is $2^{1013} - 1$. The probability that the product is odd is $\frac{2^{1013} - 1}{2^{2026} - 1}$. The probability that the product is even is $1 - \frac{2^{1013} - 1}{2^{2026} - 1} = \frac{(2^{2026} - 1) - (2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1} = \frac{2^{2026} - 2^{1013}}{2^{2026} - 1}$. Factoring out $2^{1013}$ from the numerator gives the final answer: $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1}$. Het_Prajapa

questions.questionText: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent random variables. Suppose $X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p=0.3)$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu=0,\sigma^2=100)$. Find the value of $\mathrm{Var}((2X-1)Y)$. $100$ $90$ $21$ $49$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent random variables.

Suppose $X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p=0.3)$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu=0,\sigma^2=100)$.

Find the value of $\mathrm{Var}((2X-1)Y)$.

  1. $100$
     
  2. $90$
     
  3. $21$
     
  4. $49$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Find the expected value and variance of X and Y For $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p = 0.3)$: $E[X] = p = 0.3$ $\text{Var}(X) = p(1-p) = 0.3 \times (1-0.3) = 0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21$ For $Y \sim N(\mu = 0, \sigma^2 = 100)$: $E[Y] = \mu = 0$ $\text{Var}(Y) = \sigma^2 = 100$ Step 2: Use the property of independence to find E[XY] and E[X²] Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$. [ 1 ] $E[XY] = 0.3 \times 0 = 0$ To find $\text{Var}((2X-1)Y)$, we will use the formula $\text{Var}(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2$. First, find $E[(2X-1)Y]$: $E[(2X-1)Y] = E[2XY - Y] = 2E[XY] - E[Y]$ $E[(2X-1)Y] = 2 \times 0 - 0 = 0$ Step 3: Calculate E[((2X-1)Y)²] $E[((2X-1)Y)^2] = E[(4X^2 - 4X + 1)Y^2] = E[(4(X^2 - X) + 1)Y^2]$ Since $X$ is a Bernoulli random variable, $X^2 = X$ (as $0^2=0$ and $1^2=1$). So, $X^2 - X = 0$. $E[((2X-1)Y)^2] = E[(4 \times 0 + 1)Y^2] = E[Y^2]$ Use the variance formula $\text{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2$ to find $E[Y^2]$: $E[Y^2] = \text{Var}(Y) + (E[Y])^2 = 100 + 0^2 = 100$

Among those who have the disease, $80\%$ test positive and $20\%$ test negative. Among those who do not have the disease, $10\%$ test positive and $90\%$ test negative. questions.questionHtml:
In a certain population, $30\%$ of the individuals have Disease $(D)$ and $70\%$ do not have the disease $(ND)$.

Among those who have the disease, $80\%$ test positive and $20\%$ test negative.

Among those who do not have the disease, $10\%$ test positive and $90\%$ test negative.

Find the probability that a person has the disease given that the test result is positive.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Define events and probabilities Let $D$ be the event that a person has the disease and $ND$ be the event that they do not. Let $P$ be the event that a person tests positive and $N$ be the event that they test negative.  We are given the following probabilities: $P(D) = 0.30$ $P(ND) = 0.70$ $P(P|D) = 0.80$ $P(N|D) = 0.20$ $P(P|ND) = 0.10$ $P(N|ND) = 0.90$ We need to find $P(D|P)$, the probability that a person has the disease given that they test positive. Step 2: Use Bayes' theorem Bayes' theorem states that $P(D|P) = \frac{P(P|D)P(D)}{P(P)}$. Step 3: Calculate the total probability of testing positive The total probability of testing positive, $P(P)$, can be found using the law of total probability: $P(P) = P(P|D)P(D) + P(P|ND)P(ND)$ $P(P) = (0.80)(0.30) + (0.10)(0.70)$ $P(P) = 0.24 + 0.07$ $P(P) = 0.31$ Step 4: Calculate the final probability Now substitute the values into Bayes' theorem: $P(D|P) = \frac{(0.80)(0.30)}{0.31}$ $P(D|P) = \frac{0.24}{0.31}$ $P(D|P) \approx

questions.questionText: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with CDF $F(x)$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE? $F(x)$ is always a positive function $F(x)$ has jump discontinuity $F(x)$ is a non-decreasing function $F(x)$ is left continuous
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with CDF $F(x)$.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. $F(x)$ is always a positive function
     
  2. $F(x)$ has jump discontinuity
     
  3. $F(x)$ is a non-decreasing function
     
  4. $F(x)$ is left continuous
questions.explanation: Answer: (B) F(x) has jump discontinuity and (C) F(x) is a non-decreasing function The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of any random variable, whether discrete or continuous, is always a non-decreasing function. Therefore, statement C is true. For a discrete random variable, the CDF is a step function. It increases in jumps at the points where the random variable has a non-zero probability. These jumps are defined as jump discontinuities. Therefore, statement B is true. Statement A is false because $F(x)$ is defined as a probability and ranges from 0 to 1, so it is non-negative, but not always strictly positive (it is 0 for values below the minimum possible value of the random variable). Statement D is false because the CDF of a discrete random variable is always right-continuous, not left-continuous. The $t_1$ distribution is also known as the Cauchy distribution. Part C: $G(0) = H(0)$ Both the standard normal distribution and the t-distribution (including $t_1$) are symmetric around zero. questions.questionText: Let $X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. Given that $P(X>5)=0.35$. Find the value of $P(X>10 \mid X>5)$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. Given that $P(X>5)=0.35$.

Find the value of $P(X>10 \mid X>5)$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Understand the memoryless property The exponential distribution is memoryless, meaning that the probability of a future event does not depend on past events, given that the past event has already occurred. Mathematically, for $s, t > 0$, the property is expressed as $P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$. Step 2: Apply the property In this problem, we have $s = 5$ and $t = 5$. We want to find $P(X > 10 \mid X > 5)$, which can be written as $P(X > 5+5 \mid X > 5)$. Step 3: Use the given information According to the memoryless property, $P(X > 5+5 \mid X > 5) = P(X > 5)$. We are given that $P(X > 5) = 0.35$. Answer: The value of $P(X > 10 \mid X > 5)$ is $\mathbf{0.35}$. $$
\begin{aligned}
P(X=1)=P(X=2)=P(X=5)=P(X=7) &= \frac{1}{6} \\
P(X=3)=P(X=4)=P(X=6)=P(X=8) &= \frac{1}{12}

questions.explanation: E[X] = ∑XP(X)         = x*p(x=1) + x*p(x=2) + x*p(x=3) + x*p(x=4) + x*p(x=5) + x*p(x=6) + x*p(x=7) + x*p(x=8)         = 1(1/6) + 2(1/6) + 3(1/12) + 4(1/12) + 5(1/6) + 6(1/12) + 7(1/6) + 8(1/12)         = 1/6(1+2+5+7) + 1/12(3+4+6+8)         = 15/6 + 21/12         = 2.5 + 1.75  E[X] = 4.25 Shadz_Shadz answered Feb 11 • edited Feb 11 by Shadz_Shadz Shadz_Shadz comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​​It is given that $P(X \geq 2)=0.25$ for an exponentially distributed random variable $X$ with $E[X]=\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, where $E[X]$ denotes the expectation of $X$. What is the value of $\lambda$ ? (ln denotes natural logarithm)

  2. $\ln 4$
  3. $\ln 3$
  4. $\ln 0.25$
questions.explanation: Using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Exponential Random Variable with parameter \(\lambda\): \[ F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, & x \geq 0 \\ 0, & x < 0 \end{cases} \] We want to find \(\lambda\) given that: \[ \begin{aligned} P(X \geq 2) &= 1 - P(X < 2) \\ &= 1 - F_X(2) \\ &= 1 - (1 - e^{-2\lambda}) \\ &= e^{-2\lambda} \end{aligned} \] This probability value is already given: \[ e^{-2\lambda} = 0.25 \] Taking the natural logarithm on both sides: \[ \begin{aligned} -2\lambda \ln e &= \ln \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ -2\lambda &= \ln 1 - \ln 4 \\ -2\lambda &= -\ln 4 = -\ln 2^2 = -2 \ln 2 \\ \lambda &= \ln 2 \end{aligned} \] bruh seal answered Feb 28, 2025 • edited Feb 28, 2025 by bruh seal bruh seal comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 3 3 votes ``````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````` I have used (log base e) here as [natura

questions.questionHtml:
​​​​Consider a coin-toss experiment where the probability of head showing up is $p$. In the $i^{\text {th }}$ coin toss, let $X_{i}=1$ if head appears, and $X_{i}=0$ if tail appears. Consider
\[
\widehat{p}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}
\]
where $n$ is the total number of independent coin tosses.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. $E[\widehat{p}]=p$
  2. $E[\widehat{p}]=\dfrac{p}{n}$
  3. As $n$ increases, variance of $\widehat{p}$ decreases
  4. Variance of $\widehat{p}$ does not depend on $n$

options.label: D
options.text: Variance of $\widehat{p}$ does not depend on $n$

questions.explanation: $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$ $E[\hat{p}] = E[\frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{n} E[(X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{n} (np)$  {Binomial Distribution} $ E[\hat{p}] = p $ $Var[\hat{p}] = Var[\frac{1}{n} (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $ = \frac{1}{n^2} Var[ (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n)$] $= \frac{1}{(n^2)} (np(1-p))$  {Binomial Distribution} $= \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$ $Var[\hat{p}]$  is inversely proportional to n Correct Answer A, C

We can rewrite the first equation as: $$\alpha + \beta = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha \beta$$ So we have two cases: Case 1:  $\alpha \beta = 0$ \begin{gathered}   \alpha + \beta = (\alpha + \beta)^2 \\   \implies \alpha + \beta = 0 \; \text{or} \; 1 \end{gathered} For $\alpha \beta = 0$ and $\alpha + \beta = 0$, we get $\alpha = \beta = 0$. questions.questionText: ​​​​​​When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all distinct numbers $(i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \text{and }   6)$ is $\dfrac{1}{324}$ $\dfrac{5}{324}$ $\dfrac{7}{324}$ $\dfrac{11}{324}$
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​​When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all distinct numbers $(i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \text{and }   6)$ is

  1. $\dfrac{1}{324}$

  2. $\dfrac{5}{324}$

  3. $\dfrac{7}{324}$

  4. $\dfrac{11}{324}$
questions.explanation: We have 6 unbiased dices that are rolled simultaneously. As, dices are unbiased. Then, P(x) = $1/6$ where x $\in$ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. When a dice is rolled then any number out of 6 can show up. So, with 1 dice we have 6 possible outcomes. And, when we have 6 dices and each dices have 6 choices then total possible outcomes = $6^{6}$. Total cases : $6^{6}$. Now, we want different numbers on all 6 dices. So, combination like these are our feasible cases : (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), (1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6), (2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1) , (6, 1, 3, 5. 4, 2), - - - - - - - - - - , (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) How many such feasible case? It will be 6! = 720 Feasible cases : 6! = 720 So, Required Probability : Feasible cases / Total Cases = 6! / $6^{6}$. = 5 / 324. Hence , Option B is correct Answer.

questions.questionText: Suppose \( X \) and \( Y \) are two random variables such that \( aX + bY \) is a normal random variable for all \( a, b \) in \( \mathbf{R} \). Consider the following statements P, Q, R, and S: (P) : \( X \) is a standard normal random variable. (Q) : The conditional distribution of \( X \) given \( Y \) is normal. (R) : The conditional distribution of \( X + Y\) is normal. (S) : \( X - Y \) has mean 0. Which of the above statements ALWAYS hold TRUE? (A) both P and Q (B) both Q and R (C) both Q and S (D) both P and S
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose \( X \) and \( Y \) are two random variables such that \( aX + bY \) is a normal random variable for all \( a, b \) in \( \mathbf{R} \). Consider the following statements P, Q, R, and S:
(P) : \( X \) is a standard normal random variable.
(Q) : The conditional distribution of \( X \) given \( Y \) is normal.
(R) : The conditional distribution of \( X + Y\) is normal.
(S) : \( X - Y \) has mean 0.

Which of the above statements ALWAYS hold TRUE?
(A) both P and Q

(B) both Q and R

(C) both Q and S

(D) both P and S
questions.explanation: (B), both Q and R always hold true.   Statement P: \(X\) doesn't necessarily have to be a standard normal random variable (mean of 0 and variance of 1). It could have a different mean or variance and still satisfy the condition that \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\). Therefore, P is not always true. Statement Q: If \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\), then in particular, \(Y = 0 \cdot X + 1 \cdot Y\) is normal. This implies that the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y\) is also normal. Therefore, Q is always true. Statement R: Similar to Q, if \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\), then \(X + Y = 1 \cdot X + 1 \cdot Y\) is normal. This implies that the conditional distribution of \(X + Y\) is normal. Therefore, R is always true. Statement S: There's no guarantee that \(X - Y\) has mean 0. It could have a non-zero mean and still satisfy the condition that \(aX + bY\) is normal for all \(a, b\). Therefore, S is not always true.   rajveer43 answe

Then, since \( X \) and \( Y \) are independent, we have: \[ P(X = Y) = \sum_{k=0}^4 P(X = k) \cdot P(Y = k) \] I'll calculate this probability. questions.questionHtml: Let $X1, X2, X3, X4$ be independent exponential random variables with mean $1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4,$ respectively. Then $Y = min(X1, X2, X3, X4)$ has exponential distribution with mean equal to
questions.explanation: To find the mean of the minimum of independent exponential random variables, we can use the fact that the minimum of exponential random variables follows an exponential distribution with a rate equal to the sum of the rates of the individual exponentials. Let \(X_i\) denote the exponential random variable with mean \(1/i\) for \(i = 1, 2, 3, 4\). The rate parameter \(\lambda_i\) for each \(X_i\) is given by \(\lambda_i = 1/(1/i) = i\). The minimum \(Y = \min(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4)\) has a rate parameter \(\lambda_Y\) equal to the sum of the individual rates: \[ \lambda_Y = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \lambda_4 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. \] Therefore, \(Y\) follows an exponential distribution with mean \(1/\lambda_Y\): \[ \text{Mean of } Y = \frac{1}{\lambda_Y} = \frac{1}{10}. \] So, the mean of \(Y\) is \(\frac{1}{10}\). rajveer43 answered Jan 11, 2024 rajveer43 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): Likelihood Function: The likelihood function is the joint probability density function of the observed data, viewed as a function of the parameter \( \theta \). In this case, the \(X_i\) are independent, so the likelihood function is the product of their individual density functions: \[ L(\theta) = \prod f_X(x_i; \theta) = \theta^n \exp(-\theta \sum (x_i - 1)) \] Log-Likelihood: Taking the logarithm of the likelihood function simplifies calculations: \[ \ln L(\theta) = n \ln(\theta) - \theta \sum (x_i - 1) \] Derivative: To find the MLE, we differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \( \theta \) and set it equal to 0: \[ \frac{d}{d\theta} \ln L(\theta) = \frac{n}{\theta} - \sum (x_i - 1) = 0 \] Solve for \( \theta \): Solving for \( \theta \) gives: \[ \theta = \frac{n}{\sum (x_i - 1)} = \frac{n}{nX - n} = \frac{1}{X - 1} \]   rajveer43 answered Jan 11, 2024 rajveer43 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a

Let $X$ be a non constant positive random variable such that $E(X)=9$. Then which of the following statements is correct

A) $E(1X+1)>0.1$
   and  $P(X≥10)≤0.9$

B) $E(1X+1)<0.1$
 and $P(X≥10)≤0.9$

questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) $E(1/X+1) > 0.1$ and $P(X ≥ 10) ≤ 0.9$ . Here's the explanation: 1. $E(1/X+1) > 0.1$: Non-constant positive variable:  Since X is non-constant and always positive, 1/X will also be positive but never exceed 1 (because X is at least 1). Lower bound for expected value:  This means that E(1/X) will always be a positive number less than or equal to 1. Adding 1:  When we add 1 to E(1/X), we get a value greater than 1, which is definitely more than 0.1. Therefore, E(1/X+1) > 0.1 is always true. 2. $P(X ≥ 10) ≤ 0.9$: Expected value:  E(X) = 9 indicates that X is expected to be around 9 on average. Probability of exceeding 10:  Since X is non-constant, it can take values both below and above 9. However, the probability of it being significantly larger than 9 (like 10 or more) cannot be too high, as it would contradict the expected value. Consider a random experiment where two fair coins are tossed. Let $A$ be the event that denotes $\text{HEAD}$ on both the throws, $B$ be the event that denotes $\text{HEAD}$ on the first throw, and $C$ be the event that denotes $\text{HEAD}$ on the second throw. questions.explanation: 2 Fair coins are tossed simultaneously. So, the sample space(S) is given by : S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.   Let,  A  be the event that denotes  HEAD on both the throws.  Let, B be the event that denotes  HEAD on the first throw. Let, C be the event that denotes  HEAD on the second throw.   For, Event A (Head on both coins), only one case is feasible which is HH.  $\therefore$  P(A) = 1 / 4 For, Event B (Head on first coins), only two cases are feasible which is HH, HT.  $\therefore$  P(B) = 1 / 2 For, Event C (Head on second coins), only one case is feasible which is HH, TH.  $\therefore$  P(C) = 1 / 2   NOTE : Two or more events are said to be independent, when the occurrence of one event does not  affect the occurrence of other event. In case of Independent Events : P(A $\cap$ B) = P(A) . P(B)   Let’s check options one by one :   Option – A) A & B

questions.questionText: In an examination, a student can choose the order in which two questions ($\textsf{QuesA}$ and $\textsf{QuesB}$) must be attempted. If the first question is answered wrong, the student gets zero marks. If the first question is answered correctly and the second question is not answered correctly, the student gets the marks only for the first question. If both the questions are answered correctly, the student gets the sum of the marks of the two questions. The following table shows the probability of correctly answering a question and the marks of the question respectively. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{question} & \text{probabilty of answering correctly} & \text{marks} \\ \hline \textsf{QuesA} & 0.8 & 10 \\ \textsf{QuesB} & 0.5 & 20 \end{array}$$ Assuming that the student always wants to maximize her expected marks in the examination, in which order should she attempt  the questions and what is the expected marks for that order (assume that the questions are independent)? First $\textsf{QuesA}$ and then $\textsf{QuesB}$. Expected marks $14$. First $\textsf{QuesB}$ and then $\textsf{QuesA}$. Expected marks $14$. First $\textsf{QuesB}$ and then $\textsf{QuesA}$. Expected marks $22$. First $\textsf{QuesA}$ and then $\textsf{QuesB}$. Expected marks $16$.
questions.questionHtml:
In an examination, a student can choose the order in which two questions ($\textsf{QuesA}$ and $\textsf{QuesB}$) must be attempted.

  • If the first question is answered wrong, the student gets zero marks.
  • If the first question is answered correctly and the second question is not answered correctly, the student gets the marks only for the first question.
  • If both the questions are answered correctly, the student gets the sum of the marks of the two questions.

The following table shows the probability of correctly answering a question and the marks of the question respectively.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{question} & \text{probabilty of answering correctly} & \text{marks} \\ \hline \textsf{QuesA} & 0.8 & 10 \\ \textsf{QuesB} & 0.5 & 20 \end{array}$$

Assuming that the student always wants to maximize her expected marks in the examination, in which order should she attempt  the questions and what is the expected marks for that order (assume that the questions are independent)?

  1. First $\textsf{QuesA}$ and then $\textsf{QuesB}$. Expected marks $14$.
  2. First $\textsf{QuesB}$ and then $\textsf{QuesA}$. Expected marks $14$.
  3. First $\textsf{QuesB}$ and then $\textsf{QuesA}$. Expected marks $22$.
  4. First $\textsf{QuesA}$ and then $\textsf{QuesB}$. Expected marks $16$.

questions.questionHtml: The lifetime of a component of a certain type is a random variable whose probability density function is exponentially distributed with parameter $2$. codeBlocks:
The lifetime X of a component follows an exponential distribution:

X∼Exponential(λ=2)

Expected Lifetime For an exponential distribution:

E[X]=1/λ=1/0.5

Find P(X>E[X])=P(X>0.5)

Use the exponential probability formula:

P(X>x)=e^−λx

Substitute x=0.5

P(X>0.5)=e^−2⋅0.5 = e^-1 ≈ 0.36

questions.explanation: Remember: In Python, default arguments are evaluated only once at the time of function definition.   If the default argument is mutable (like a list), the same object is reused across function calls. First call: \[ \texttt{append_to_lst(1)} \rightarrow [1] \] Second call (same default list reused): \[ \texttt{append_to_lst(2)} \rightarrow [1, 2] \] Third call (new empty list passed explicitly): \[ \texttt{append_to_lst(3, [])} \rightarrow [3] \] Final Output: \[ [1] \] \[ [1, 2] \] \[ [3] \] Hence, the correct option is: \[ {(B)} \]

questions.questionText: ​​​​​​A recursive function in Python is given. def mystery(n): if n <= 0: return 1 else: return mystery(n-1) + mystery(n-2) Now, consider the following function call: mystery(4) Assume that a typical runtime stack is used to manage function calls. Each function call is pushed onto the stack and removed only after it finishes execution. Which of the following options denotes the total number of function calls (i.e., the total number of stack activations), including the initial call, to compute mystery$(4)?$ $5$ $9$ $15$ $17$
questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​​A recursive function in Python is given.

def mystery(n):
    if n <= 0:
        return 1
    else:
        return mystery(n-1) + mystery(n-2)

Now, consider the following function call:

mystery(4)

Assume that a typical runtime stack is used to manage function calls. Each function call is pushed onto the stack and removed only after it finishes execution.

Which of the following options denotes the total number of function calls (i.e., the total number of stack activations), including the initial call, to compute mystery$(4)?$

  1. $5$
  2. $9$
  3. $15$
  4. $17$
questions.explanation: \[ \texttt{mystery(4)}. \]Recursion Expansion Since $n > 0$, each call generates two further calls: \[ m(n) \rightarrow m(n-1) + m(n-2) \] Expanding m(4) fully down to the base cases: \[ \begin{array}{c}\hspace{1.7cm} m(4) \\[6pt] \begin{array}{cc}\ m(3) & m(2) \\[6pt] \begin{array}{cc} m(2) & \hspace{1cm} m(1) \end{array} & \begin{array}{cc} m(1) & \hspace{1cm}m(0) \end{array} \\[12pt] \begin{array}{cccc} \hspace{1px}m(1) & m(0) & m(0) & m(-1) \end{array} \\[12pt] \begin{array}{cccccc}  \hspace{-1cm} m(-1) & m(0)\ \hspace{1.5cm}& m(-1) & m(0) \end{array} \end{array} \end{array} \] Count all nodes: \[ \begin{aligned} m(4) &: 1 \\ m(3) &: 1 \\ m(2) &: 2 \\ m(1) &: 3 \\ m(0) &: 5 \\ m(-1) &: 3 \\ \end{aligned} \] \[ \text{Total calls} = 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 15 \] \[ \boxed{\text{Total number of function calls} = 15} \] \[ \boxed{\text{Correct option: (C)}} \]

codeBlocks:

    x = []
    def inner(val):
        x.append(val)
        return x
    return inner

f2 = outer()

questions.explanation: The function outer creates a list x and defines another function inner inside it. The function inner uses the variable x and returns it after appending a value. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from its enclosing function even after the enclosing function has finished execution. When outer() is called, it creates a new list x and returns the function inner. The returned function keeps a reference to that specific x. This preserved binding between the function and its surrounding state is called a closure. When f1 = outer() a new list is created: x₁ = [] When f2 = outer() another new list is created: x₂ = [] Thus, f1 and f2 do not share the same list. Execution of print statements: Line P: f1(10) x₁ becomes \[ [10] \] Output: [10] Line Q: f1(20) x₁ becomes \[ [10, 20] \] Output: [10, 20] Line R: f2(30) x₂ becomes \[ [30] \] Output: [30] Line S: f1(40) x₁ becomes \[ [10, 20, 40] \] Output: [10, 20, 40] Checking options: (A) f1 and f2 share the same list x  False

questions.explanation: Only P1 will compile without any error. In the semantic phase, the C compiler GCC resolves variables by scope hierarchy which initially search in the local scope (defined within a block) and if the variable is not found then only proceeds to global scope.  As in P1 within the main function scope, a is only defined once locally, compiler will be able to resolve reference of a without proceeding to check global scope where a different declaration of a exists. Whereas, in both option B and C, there are two different definition for a within the local scope, hence the compiler wont be able to resolve which defination should be considered for a, hence compilation will fail in any case where re-declaration happens within the same scope. questions.explanation: Answer: B The key to this problem is understanding how default arguments are handled in Python. When lst=[] is used as a default argument, the same list object is created only once when the function is defined, not every time the function is called. Subsequent calls to the function without providing a new list will reuse and modify this single, shared list object.  The first call, append_to_lst(1), uses the default list. The list becomes [1], and [1] is printed. The second call, append_to_lst(2), again uses the same default list object. The value 2 is appended to the existing list, making it [1, 2], and [1, 2] is printed. The third call, append_to_lst(3, []), explicitly provides a new , empty list ([]) as an argument. The value 3 is appended to this new list, making it [3], and [3] is printed. The output will therefore be: [1] [1, 2] [3] Het_Prajapati answered Feb 17 Het_Prajapati comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Voting & Accepting an a

questions.explanation: Let's break down the sorting problem step-by-step for the array A=[1,2,3,5,4] where n=5. 1. Bubble Sort (N1​) Standard Bubble Sort (without the "early exit" optimized flag) always performs 2n(n−1)​ comparisons. Calculations : (5×(5−1)) ​/2 =10. Result : N1​=10. 2. Insertion Sort (N2​) Insertion Sort comparisons depend on the current state of the array. We take each element (starting from the second) and compare it with the sorted elements to its left. Step 1 (Element 2) : Compare '2' with '1'. (1 comparison). Array: [1,2,3,5,4] Step 2 (Element 3) : Compare '3' with '2'. (1 comparison). Array: [1,2,3,5,4] Step 3 (Element 5) : Compare '5' with '3'. (1 comparison). Array: [1,2,3,5,4] Step 4 (Element 4) : Compare '4' with '5'. (1 comparison). Since 4<5, we keep looking left. Compare '4' with '3'. (1 comparison). Since 4>3, we stop. Array becomes: [1,2,3,4,5] Total Comparisons (N2​) : 1+1+1+2=5. Evaluating the Statements A. Insertion Sort on A performs only one swap : Correct . Only

questions.questionHtml:
A binary tree has the following traversals:

  • Preorder traversal$: P, Q, S, E, R, F, G$
     
  • Inorder traversal$: S, Q, E, P, F, R, G$
     

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

  1. Node $Q$ has only one child.
     
  2. The postorder traversal is $S, E, Q, F, G, R, P$.
     
  3. The left subtree of $R$ contains node $G$.
     
  4. Node $P$ is the root of the tree.

options.label: B
options.text: The postorder traversal is $S, E, Q, F, G, R, P$.

options.label: C
options.text: The left subtree of $R$ contains node $G$.

options.label: D
options.text: Node $P$ is the root of the tree.

questions.explanation: Answer: B,D The preorder traversal is $P, Q, S, E, R, F, G$ and the inorder traversal is $S, Q, E, P, F, R, G$. A. Node $Q$ has only one child. Inorder: $S, Q, E$. $Q$ is the root of its subtree. $S$ is its left child and $E$ is its right child. This statement is false. B. The postorder traversal is $S, E, Q, F, G, R, P.$ By constructing the binary tree from the given traversals, we find that the postorder traversal (left, right, root) is indeed $S, E, Q, F, G, R, P$. This statement is true. C. The left subtree of $R$ contains node $G$. Inorder: $S, Q, E, P, F, R, G$. $R$ is a root of a subtree; $F$ is in its left subtree and $G$ is in its right subtree. This statement is false. D. Node $P$ is the root of the tree. In a preorder traversal, the first element is always the root of the tree. Thus, $P$ is the root. This statement is true. B and D are true statements Het_Prajapati answered Feb 17 Het_Prajapati comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 vot

Output at line $\verb|Q|$ is $[10,20]$. $\verb|f1|$ and $\verb|f2|$ share the same list. Output at line $\verb|S|$ is $[10,20,40]$. Output at line $\verb|R|$ is $[10,20,30]$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following Python code:

def outer():
    x = []
    def inner(val):
        x.append(val)
        return x
    return inner

Now consider:

f1 = outer()
f2 = outer()

print(f1(10))  # P
print(f1(20))  # Q
print(f2(30))  # R
print(f1(40))  # S

What will be the output of $\verb|P|$, $\verb|Q|$, $\verb|R|$, and $\verb|S|$?

  1. Output at line $\verb|Q|$ is $[10,20]$.
     
  2. $\verb|f1|$ and $\verb|f2|$ share the same list.
     
  3. Output at line $\verb|S|$ is $[10,20,40]$.
     
  4. Output at line $\verb|R|$ is $[10,20,30]$.
codeBlocks:
def outer():
    x = []
    def inner(val):
        x.append(val)
        return x
    return inner

f1 = outer()
f2 = outer()

print(f1(10))  # P
print(f1(20))  # Q
print(f2(30))  # R
print(f1(40))  # S
questions.explanation: Answer: (A) Output at line Q is and (C) Output at line S is When outer() is called, a new local variable x (an empty list) is created each time. f1 and f2 are two separate instances of the inner function, each with its own closure over a distinct x list created by their respective calls to outer(). f1(10) appends 10 to f1's list x, so P is [10]. f1(20) appends 20 to the same f1 list x, so Q is [10, 20]. f2(30) appends 30 to f2's separate list x, so R is [30]. f1(40) appends 40 to the same f1 list x, so S is [10, 20, 40]. Based on this, options A and C are correct statements. Option B is incorrect because f1 and f2 have separate lists. Option D is incorrect because R's output is [30].

{

questions.explanation: First of all understand what both of the functions are really doing. int bar(int n) { if (n == 1) return 0; else return 1 + bar(n/2); } Each call divides $n$ by $2$ and adds $1$ until it reaches $1.$ So, basically, it is finding $\lfloor \log_2n \rfloor.$ $\therefore \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid black]{bar(n) = \lfloor \log_2n \rfloor}$          $-$ $(1)$ int foo(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; else return 1 + foo(bar(n)); } So, $foo(n) = 1 + foo(bar(n))$, using first equation we can write, $\therefore \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid black]{foo(n) = 1 + foo(\lfloor \log_2n \rfloor)}$          $-$ $(2)$ Base case : $foo(0) = 0$ Now, we need to find $n$ such that, $foo(n)=5$. So, we can open up $foo(n)$ in following way :  Now, using base case we can say that, for $foo(log~log~log~log~log~n) = 0 $ $log~log~log~log~log~n = 0$ So, from this we can find $n$ as follows :  $\mathbf{\therefore n = 2^{16} = 65536}$ benzene06 answered

questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C program:

#include <stdio.h>

int g(int n) {
    return (n+10);
}

int f(int n) {
    return g(n*2);
}

int main() {
    int sum, n;
    sum=0;
    for (n=1; n<3; n++)
         sum += g(f(n));
    printf ("%d", sum);
    return 0;
}

The output of the given C program is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Let us first expand the expression given in the main function; sum+=g(f(n)) can be written as sum=sum+g(f(n)) now, coming to the for loops, it is run two times. when $n=1,1<3:T$,it is called as $0+g(f(1))$. when $f(1)$ is called it return $g(2)$ which is go to function g(n) where it is executed $10+2$ and return $12$ to main fuction.again sum=0+g(12), now we call one more time $g(n)$ this time it return $10+12=22$.Therefore final value of the sum after the first iteration is $22.$ now increment $n++$ gives $n=2,2<3:T$, loop will run one more time as $sum=22+g(f(2))$ when $f(2)$ is called it return g(4) which go to function $g(4)$ and it return as $10+4=14$ to main fuciton. so $sum=22+g(14)$, now $g(14)$ will return again $10+14=24$. so the final value of the sum is $22+24=46$ so the output of the given program is $46.$ Hira Thakur answered Feb 28, 2025 Hira Thakur comment Share Follow See all 3 Comments 3 3 Comments reply Om Dwivedi commented Aug 9, 2025 reply Follow flag are yr

So the string "Hello World!" gets copied over the beginning of the array. stringcopy function doesn't copy the null character '\0' that ends the string. So after copying, the string is not properly terminated. That means: printf("%s", a); doesn’t know where to stop, and might keep printing garbage from memory after "Hello World!" . When we call the function $foo(z, b)$, the first argument is passed as the address of the variable $a$, and the second argument is passed as the value of $b$, which is assigned to the variable $x$. Inside the $foo()$ function, the line $*p = x$ simply assigns the value of $x$ to the pointer $p$ (where $*p$ is treated as a double pointer). questions.questionText: Consider the following $\text{ANSI C}$ program. #include <stdio.h> int main() { int arr[4][5]; int i, j; for (i=0; i<4; i++) ​​​​​​{ for (j=0; j<5; j++) { arr[i][j] = 10 * i + j; } } printf(“%d”, *(arr[1]+9)); return 0; } What is the output of the above program? $14$ $20$ $24$ $30$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following $\text{ANSI C}$ program.

#include <stdio.h>
int main() 
{
    int arr[4][5];
    int  i, j;
    for (i=0; i<4; i++) 
    ​​​​​​{
        for (j=0; j<5; j++) 
        {
            arr[i][j] = 10 * i + j;
        }
    }
    printf(“%d”, *(arr[1]+9));
    return 0;
}

What is the output of the above program?

  1. $14$
  2. $20$
  3. $24$
  4. $30$
codeBlocks:
arr[1]+9 = *(arr+1) + 9 //arr is again a pointer but to the 2D array arr[4][5]

arr+1 = arr + sizeof(*arr)
      = arr + 5 * sizeof (int)
     
*(arr+1)+9 = arr + 5 * sizeof(int) + sizeof(**arr) * 9
//* operator in *(arr+1) just changes the type of the pointer here
        = arr + 5 * sizeof(int) + 9 * sizeof(int)
        = arr + 14 * sizeof(int)

​​​​​Consider the following$\text{ ANSI C}$ program.

#include <stdio.h>
int main()
{
    int i, j, count;
    count=0;

    for (j=-3; j<=3; j++)
    {
        if (( j >= 0) && (i++))
            count = count + j;
    }
    count = count +i;
    printf("%d", count);
    return 0;
}

  1. The program will not compile successfully
  2. The program will compile successfully and output $10$ when executed

questions.excerpt: int main(){float sum, i = 1.0, j = 2.0;while (i/j  0.0625){j = j + j;printf("%f", i+j);}}The number of times printf statement is executed is:
questions.questionText: int main() { float sum, i = 1.0, j = 2.0; while (i/j > 0.0625) { j = j + j; printf("%f", i+j); } } The number of times printf statement is executed is:
questions.questionHtml:
int main()
{
float sum, i = 1.0, j = 2.0;
while (i/j > 0.0625)
{
j = j + j;
printf("%f", i+j);
}
}

The number of times printf statement is executed is:
questions.explanation: According to the above example, the loop will run 5 times as the values of i/j is 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.0625 respectively. But in the actual GATE 2019 question the values were swapped and according to that, the loop will run 3 times. Kritika14 answered Feb 7, 2019 Kritika14 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes In the current question, printf will be executed  3 times . In Gate 2019 question paper however, the original question was: int main() {   float sum = 0.0, j = 1.0, i = 2.0 ;   while (i / j > 0.0625)   {     j = j + j;     sum = sum + i/j;     printf("%f\n", sum);   } } In the above scenario, printf will be executed  5 times Padhi98 answered May 12, 2020 Padhi98 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider two distinct positive real numbers $m, n$, with $m>n$. Let $x=n^{\log _{10}(m)}$ and $y=m^{\log _{10}(n)}$. The relation between $x$ and $y$ is $\_\_\_\_$. $x>y$ $x<y$ $x=y$ $x=\log _{10}(y)$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider two distinct positive real numbers $m, n$, with $m>n$. Let $x=n^{\log _{10}(m)}$ and $y=m^{\log _{10}(n)}$. The relation between $x$ and $y$ is $\_\_\_\_$.

  1. $x>y$
  2. $x<y$
  3. $x=y$
  4. $x=\log _{10}(y)$
questions.explanation: Given \[ x = n^{\log_{10} m}, \quad y = m^{\log_{10} n}. \] Use the logarithmic identity \[ a^{\log_b c} = c^{\log_b a}, \] Interchanging \(m\) and \(n\) for x using the above identity, we get \[ n^{\log_{10} m} = m^{\log_{10} n}. \] which is same as y. Hence, \[ x = y. \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 26 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes It is given that $ x = n^ {\log_{10} m}$ and $y = m^ {\log_{10} n}$ Applying log with base 10 on both sides, we get $\log_{10} x = \log_{10} m . \log_{10} n$ and $\log_{10} y = \log_{10} n . \log_{10} m$ Comparing above two equations we get, $\log_{10} x = \log_{10} y$ which means $x = y$ Hence, Answer is C. sri321 answered Feb 24 sri321 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:

questions.explanation: A day can either be cloudy or sunny only. If probability of a day being cloudy is 0.5 then it being sunny is also 0.5. Use binomial ditribution : Out of 4 days, choose 3 days for cloudy. $\binom{4}{3}*(\frac{1}{2})^{3}(\frac{1}{2}) = 4*(\frac{1}{16}) = \frac{1}{4}$ Franz Kafka answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 25 by Misbah Ghaya Franz Kafka comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote The prob for cloudy = 1/2, therfore for sunny = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2. Thus equal likely of the events. Using the formula nCk*p^k*(1-p)^n-k p = 0.5 [probabilty of the event] n = 4 [given days] k = 3 [conditon given, here 3 days to be cloudy] P(K==3) = 4C3 x 0.5^3 x 0.5^(4-3)               = (4x3x2x1/3x2x1) x 1/8 x 1/2               = 4/16               = 1/4 Vaibhavshukl

questions.questionText: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers $1,2,3,4,5$, and $6$ is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$ $\frac{3}{36}$ $\frac{13}{36}$ $\frac{15}{36}$ $\frac{19}{36}$
questions.questionHtml:
An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers $1,2,3,4,5$, and $6$ is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$

  1. $\frac{3}{36}$
  2. $\frac{13}{36}$
  3. $\frac{15}{36}$
  4. $\frac{19}{36}$
questions.explanation: When a six-faced die is rolled twice, the total number of possible outcomes in the sample space $S$ is: $n(S) = 6 \times 6 = 36$ here we use six-sided dice as a pair, then the minimum possible sum will be $1+1=2$, and the maximum will be $6+6=12$. so the required prime numbers between 2 and 12 are: $\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11\}$. Now, we have to find the pairs $(x, y)$ that result in these sums: Sum = 2: $(1, 1) \rightarrow \mathbf{1 \text{ possibilities}}$ Sum = 3: $(1, 2), (2, 1) \rightarrow \mathbf{2 \text{ possibilities}}$ Sum = 5: $(1, 4), (4, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2) \rightarrow \mathbf{4 \text{ possibilities}}$ Sum = 7: $(1, 6), (6, 1), (2, 5), (5, 2), (3, 4), (4, 3) \rightarrow \mathbf{6 \text{ possibilities}}$ Sum = 11: $(5, 6), (6, 5) \rightarrow \mathbf{2 \text{ possibilities}}$ therefore total favorable outcome is: $n(E) = 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15$ $P(\text{Sum is Prime}) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)} = \frac{15}{36}$ Option $(C)$ is correct.

questions.questionHtml:
An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with $1,2,3,4,5$ and 6 is rolled twice.
What is the probability that the number appearing in the second roll is an integer multiple of the number appearing in the first roll?

  1. $\frac{1}{6}$
     
  2. $\frac{5}{18}$
     
  3. $\frac{7}{18}$
     
  4. $\frac{5}{6}$
questions.explanation: $a$ = first roll, $b$ = second roll. We need $b$ to be a multiple of $a$, i.e., $b = ka$ for some integer $k$. Total outcomes $= 6 \times 6 = 36$. If $a=1$, every value of $b$ is allowed $\Rightarrow 6$ outcomes. If $a=2$, $b=2,4,6 \Rightarrow 3$ outcomes. If $a=3$, $b=3,6 \Rightarrow 2$ outcomes. If $a=4$, $b=4 \Rightarrow 1$ outcome. If $a=5$, $b=5 \Rightarrow 1$ outcome. If $a=6$, $b=6 \Rightarrow 1$ outcome. Total favourable outcomes $= 6+3+2+1+1+1 = 14$. $P = \dfrac{14}{36} = \dfrac{7}{18}$. pebkac20 answered Feb 11 pebkac20 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Weight of a person can be expressed as a function of their age. The function usually varies from person to person. Suppose this function is identical for two brothers, and it monotonically increases till the age of 50 years and then it monotonically decreases. Let $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ (in years) denote the ages of the brothers and $a_{1} < a_{2}$. Which one of the following statements is correct about their age on the day when they attain the same weight? $a_{1} < a_{2} < 50$ $a_{1} < 50 < a_{2}$ $50 < a_{1} < a_{2}$ Either $a_{1}=50$ or $a_{2}=50$
questions.questionHtml:
Weight of a person can be expressed as a function of their age. The function usually varies from person to person. Suppose this function is identical for two brothers, and it monotonically increases till the age of 50 years and then it monotonically decreases. Let $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ (in years) denote the ages of the brothers and $a_{1} < a_{2}$.

Which one of the following statements is correct about their age on the day when they attain the same weight?

  1. $a_{1} < a_{2} < 50$
  2. $a_{1} < 50 < a_{2}$
  3. $50 < a_{1} < a_{2}$
  4. Either $a_{1}=50$ or $a_{2}=50$
questions.explanation: We are given that the weight function $W(a)$ behaves as follows: Monotonically Increases: For $a < 50$. This means if age increases, weight increases. Peak: The function reaches its maximum at $a = 50$. Monotonically Decreases: For $a > 50$. This means if age increases, weight decreases. Let the ages of the two brothers be $a_1$ and $a_2$. We are told that on a specific day, they have the same weight. Therefore: $$W(a_1) = W(a_2)$$ We are also given that $a_1 < a_2$. Let's look at the three possible regions for the ages relative to the peak at 50 years: Case A: Both brothers are younger than 50 ($a_1 < a_2 < 50$) Since the function is strictly increasing in this range, if $a_1 < a_2$, then $W(a_1)$ must be less than $W(a_2)$. They cannot have the same weight. This rules out option (A). Case C: Both brothers are older than 50 ($50 < a_1 < a_2$) Since the function is strictly decreasing in this range, if $a_1 < a_2$, then $W(a_1)$ must be greater than $W(a_2)$

Which one of the following options is correct for the given data in the table?

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Iteration (i)} & \text{0} & \text{1} & \text{2} & \text{3}  \\  \hline
\text{Input (I)} & \text{20} & \text{-4} & \text{10} & \text{15}  \\  \hline
\text{Output (X)} & \text{20} & \text{16} & \text{26} & \text{41}  \\  \hline \text{Output (Y)} & \text{20} & \text{-80} & \text{-800} & \text{-12000}  \\  \hline
\end{array}$$

  2. $X(i) = X(i-1)I(i); \: \: Y(i) = Y(i-1)+I(i); \: \: i>0$
  3. $X(i) = X(i-1)I(i); \: \: Y(i) = Y(i-1)I(i); \: \: i>0$

questions.explanation: \[X(i) = X(i-1) + I(i)\]\[X(1) = X(0) + I(1) = 20 + (-4) = 16, \quad \text{satisfied}\]\[X(2) = X(1) + I(2) = 16 + 10 = 26, \quad \text{satisfied}\]\[X(3) = X(2) + I(3) = 26 + 15 = 41, \quad \text{satisfied}\] \[Y(i) = Y(i-1)I(i), \quad i > 0\]\[Y(1) = Y(0) \times I(1) = (-20) \times 4 = -80, \quad \text{satisfied}\]\[Y(2) = Y(1) \times I(2) = (-80) \times 10 = -800, \quad \text{satisfied}\]\[Y(3) = Y(2) \times I(3) = (-800) \times 15 = -12000, \quad \text{satisfied}\] BhavdeepSinghNijhawa answered Feb 28, 2025 BhavdeepSinghNijhawa comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 3 3 votes We need to determine which of the given formulas correctly describe the transformation from Input I(i)I(i)I(i) to Output X(i)X(i)X(i) and Output Y(i)Y(i)Y(i). questions.questionHtml: In the Given figure, PQRS is a square of side $2$ cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of teh rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.
questions.explanation: Assume, $\angle QPL = \theta$, As,  $\angle QPS = 90$, $\angle LPS = 90- \theta$ As, $\angle LPN = 90$, $\angle SPN = \theta.$ Now, In $\triangle\; QPL$, $cos \;\theta = \dfrac{PQ}{PL}$. $PQ = 2$ $($given in question$)$ So, $cos \;\theta = \dfrac{2}{PL}$. So, $\mathbf{PL = \dfrac{2}{cos\;\theta}}$ Now, In $\triangle \; SPN$, $cos \;\theta = \dfrac{PN}{PS}$. $PS = 2$ $($given in question$)$ So, $cos \;\theta = \dfrac{PN}{2}$. So, $\mathbf{PN = 2 \cdot cos\;\theta}$ Now, Area of Rectangle $= PL \cdot PN$ $= \dfrac{2}{cos\;\theta} \cdot 2 \cdot cos\;\theta$ $= 4$ So, Area of Rectangle $\mathbf{= 4}$ Answer : $\mathbf{(D) 4}$ benzene06 answered Feb 27, 2025 • edited Mar 3, 2025 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Share Follow See all 4 Comments 4 4 Comments reply P0535_Yedidyah_Sagar commented Jul 15, 2025 reply Follow flag Nice one benzene 2 2 reply Share Haha_huh commented Jul 28, 2025 reply Follow flag Triangle PQL is similar to Triangle PNS (Angle QPL = Angle NPS

questions.questionText: A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled   ‘  $1$  ’ , ‘  $2$  ’ , ‘  $3$  ’ , ‘  $4$  ’ , ‘  $5$  ’ , and ‘  $6$  ’ , is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling ‘  $6$  ’  exactly once? $\dfrac{75}{216}$ $\dfrac{1}{6}$ $\dfrac{1}{18}$ $\dfrac{25}{216}$
questions.questionHtml:
A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled  ‘ $1$ ’, ‘ $2$ ’, ‘ $3$ ’, ‘ $4$ ’, ‘ $5$ ’, and ‘ $6$ ’, is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling ‘ $6$ ’ exactly once?

  1. $\dfrac{75}{216}$

  2. $\dfrac{1}{6}$

  3. $\dfrac{1}{18}$

  4. $\dfrac{25}{216}$
questions.explanation: (A) 75 / 216 Probability of getting 6 on a dice = 1/6 Probability of NOT getting 6 on a dice = 5/6 (1) Getting 6 on first roll ONLY = (1/6)*(5/6)*(5/6)   [ exactly 1 six so if we get 6 on first roll, there should not be any 6 in next 2 roll ] = 25/216 (2) Getting 6 on second roll ONLY = (5/6)*(1/6)*(5/6) = 25/216 (3) Getting 6 on third roll ONLY = (5/6)*(5/6)*(1/6) = 25/216 Probability of rolling exactly one 6 = (25/216) + (25/216) + (25/216) = 75/216 param_modi answered Feb 28, 2025 param_modi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 18 18 votes Option A is correct.

questions.questionText: For positive non-zero real variables $p$ and $q$, if $\log \left(p^2+q^2\right)=\log p+\log q+2 \log 3,$ then, the value of $\frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2 q^2}$ is $79$ $81$ $9$ $83$
questions.questionHtml:
For positive non-zero real variables $p$ and $q$, if

$\log \left(p^2+q^2\right)=\log p+\log q+2 \log 3,$

then, the value of $\frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2 q^2}$ is

  1. $79$
  2. $81$
  3. $9$
  4. $83$
questions.explanation: Given that, $\log(p^2 + q^2) = \log p + \log q + 2 \log 3$ We can assume it's a $\log$ base $10$ $\log_{10}(p^2 + q^2) = \log_{10} p + \log_{10} q + 2 \log_{10} 3$ $\log_{10}(p^2 + q^2) = \log_{10} (pq) + \log_{10} 3^2$ $\log_{10}(p^2 + q^2) = \log_{10} (9pq) $ $p^2+q^2 = 9pq$ We can take a square on both sides. $(p^2+q^2)^2 = (9pq)^2$ $p^4 + q^4 + 2p^2q^2 = 81p^2q^2$ $p^4 + q^4  = 81p^2q^2 - 2p^2q^2$ $p^4 + q^4  = 79p^2q^2$ $\dfrac{p^4 + q^4}{p^2q^2} = 79$ Correct Answer: A

The typical energy density $(\mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{g})$ of these macronutrients is given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Macronutrient} & \text{Energy density (kcal/g)}  \\  \hline \text{Carbohydrates} & \text{4}  \\  \hline \text{Proteins} & \text{4}  \\  \hline \text{Unsaturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Saturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Trans fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \end{array}$$ The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is  $44.4$ $77.8$ $100$ $3,600$
questions.questionHtml:
The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical $2,000\; \mathrm{kcal}$ diet of a person.

The typical energy density $(\mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{g})$ of these macronutrients is given in the table.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline
\text{Macronutrient} & \text{Energy density (kcal/g)}  \\  \hline
\text{Carbohydrates} & \text{4}  \\  \hline
\text{Proteins} & \text{4}  \\  \hline \text{Unsaturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Saturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Trans fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline
\end{array}$$

The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is 

  1. $44.4$
  2. $77.8$
  3. $100$
  4. $3,600$
questions.explanation: To determine the total fat (all three types) in grams that a person consumes based on the provided pie chart and energy density table, we will follow these steps: Solution By Steps Step 1: Calculate Total Energy from Each Macronutrient The total energy intake is 2,000 kcal. We will calculate the energy contribution from each macronutrient based on their percentage. Carbohydrates: 35% of 2000 kcal = 0.35 * 2000 = 700 kcal Proteins: 20% of 2000 kcal = 0.20 * 2000 = 400 kcal Unsaturated fat: 20% of 2000 kcal = 0.20 * 2000 = 400 kcal Saturated fat: 20% of 2000 kcal = 0.20 * 2000 = 400 kcal Trans fat: 5% of 2000 kcal = 0.05 * 2000 = 100 kcal Step 2: Calculate Grams of Each Macronutrient Using the energy density values, we convert kcal to grams. Carbohydrates: 700 kcal / 4 kcal/g = 175 g Proteins: 400 kcal / 4 kcal/g = 100 g Unsaturated fat: 400 kcal / 9 kcal/g = 44.44 g Saturated fat: 400 kcal / 9 kcal/g = 44.44 g Trans fat: 100 kcal / 9 kcal/g = 11.11 g Step 3: Calculate Total Fat in Gram

questions.questionText: Consider two functions of time $(t),$ $$ \begin{gathered} f(t)=0.01 t^2 \\ g(t)=4 t \end{gathered} $$ where $0<t<\infty.$ Now consider the following two statements: For some $t>0, g(t)>f(t)$. There exists a $T,$ such that $f(t)>g(t)$ for all $t>T$. Which one of the following options is $\text{TRUE}?$ only (i) is correct only (ii) is correct both (i) and (ii) are correct neither (i) nor (ii) is correct
questions.questionHtml:
Consider two functions of time $(t),$
$$
\begin{gathered}
f(t)=0.01 t^2 \\
g(t)=4 t
\end{gathered}
$$
where $0<t<\infty.$

Now consider the following two statements:

  1. For some $t>0, g(t)>f(t)$.
  2. There exists a $T,$ such that $f(t)>g(t)$ for all $t>T$.

Which one of the following options is $\text{TRUE}?$

  1. only (i) is correct
  2. only (ii) is correct
  3. both (i) and (ii) are correct
  4. neither (i) nor (ii) is correct
questions.explanation: Given, $f(t)=0.01t^{2}$ $g(t)=4t$ and $0< t< \infty$ for option $(i)$, take $t=1$,Now, $f(1)=0.01$ $g(1)=4$, So, here exists some $t$ ,t=1 , for which $g(t)>f(t).$ So $(i)$ is true . for option $(ii)$,There exists some $ T=1000$(say) .Now any $t>T$ , $f(t)>g(t)$ . So option (II) is also true . This question is nothing but Big oh definition .  $g(t)\leq cf(t)$ for all $t>T$ and $c>0$ . https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation So correct option is (C) .

questions.explanation: When we define "functions", we should also have to define domain and co-domain but sometimes it is not defined in gate. Here, domain is defined but co-domain is not defined, so I am taking it as set of real numbers. So, we have $f:\mathcal{R} \rightarrow \mathcal{R}$ and $g:\mathcal{R} \rightarrow \mathcal{R}$ Now, two functions $f$ and $g$ are equal if they have the same domain and codomain and for every element $x$ in the domain (because dom(f)=dom(g)), $f(x)=g(x).$ for example, $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{2}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{2x}{4}$ But, here, we have given two equal functions where $x$ and $y$ may or may not be same i.e. $f(x)=g(y)$ where $x$ and $y$ belongs to the set of real numbers.  So, $\forall x,y \in \mathcal{R}, $ $f(x) = g(y)$ and it is true when all $x \in \mathcal{R}$ maps to some element, say, $c$ where $c$ belongs to set $\mathcal{R}$ which is the codomain of $f$ and similarly, all $y \in \mathcal{R}$ maps to same element $c$ where $c$ belongs to set $\mathcal{R}$

questions.questionText: Consider two cones joined at a common circular base. If we cut a plane passing through the vertices of both cones, what type of shape will be formed by the intersection of the plane with the combined cones? Rhombus Triangle Hexagon Ellipse
questions.questionHtml:
Consider two cones joined at a common circular base. If we cut a plane passing through the vertices of both cones, what type of shape will be formed by the intersection of the plane with the combined cones?

  1. Rhombus
  2. Triangle
  3. Hexagon
  4. Ellipse
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Rhombus Explanation: Let's first understand the case for a single cone. We know that a cone has a circular base with a curved surface. It possess a single vertex. Now we know that the slant height of a cone is observed to be constat when calculated from any side. If another cone is attached to this cone with a common circular base. This states that the other cone must possess a circular base with the same radius as that of the former. We assume that the cones shall have the same heights. If a cross-section is cut through this 3D figure passing through the 2 vertices, it would produce a 4 sided polygon with equal sides but with internal angle which could be 90 degree or not and equal opposite internal angles. Hence it would form a rhombus. Rhombus have these properties: Have equal length sides. Have internal angle which may or may not be 90 degree. Have equal and opposite internal angles. prithvs answered Apr 6, 2024 prithvs comment Share Follow 0 reply P

Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?
Turing machine $M$ decides the language $L \subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}$

  1. Turing machine $M$ halts on all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}$
  2. Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$
  3. Turing machine $M$ rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}-L$
  4. Turing machine $M$ accepts all input strings in $L$ and rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}-L$

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Turing machine $M$ rejects all input strings in $\{0,1\}^{*}-L$

questions.explanation: Given "Turing machine M decides the language L ⊆ {0,1}* " "A Turing machine M decides" means that the turing machine can  accept and halt on all the members of L   and  reject and halt on all the inputs that are not belonging to the language L  ie L^c which is {0,1}* - L Therefore option D is the right answer ASH1198 answered Mar 7 ASH1198 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Decider is what always halts. For members, it accepts and for non members it always rejects. There's no looping problem here. So option D is correct.

As for the remaining options, $$L(D_1) \cap L (D_2)={\epsilon}$$ as no other string apart from empty string could be in common. questions.questionHtml:
Given $L_1 \cap L_2$ is Regular and $L_2$ is Regular. Which of the following is/are always TRUE?

  1. $L_2$ complement is Context-Free.
     
  2. $L_1$ is Regular.
     
  3. $L_1 \cup L_2$ is Regular.
     
  4. $L_1$ is Context-Free.
questions.explanation: A is True. For A, we know that regular languages are closed under complementation, meaning that $L_2$ being regular implies $\bar{L}_2$ is also regular. Moreover, as every regular language is context free by definition, hence $\bar{L}_2$ is also context free. This makes A true. B is False. Here's the counterexample which satisfies both conditions. Take $L_2$ as $\phi$, and L1 as $\{a^nb^nc^n | n \geq 0 \}$. Hence, B is incorrect. Similarly, C and D are also incorrect using the same adversarial setup as above. Both L1 as well the union would equal $ \{a^nb^nc^n | n \geq 0 \}$ (both are CSLs).

questions.questionHtml:
​​​​Let $G_{1}, G_{2}$ be Context Free Grammars (CFGs) and $R$ be a regular expression. For a grammar $G$, let $L(G)$ denote the language generated by $G$.

Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?

  1. Is $L\left(G_{1}\right)=L\left(G_{2}\right) ?$
  2. Is $L\left(G_{1}\right) \cap L\left(G_{2}\right)=\emptyset$ ?
  3. Is $L\left(G_{1}\right)=L(R) ?$
  4. Is $L\left(G_{1}\right)=\emptyset$ ?
questions.explanation: \( L(G_1) = L(G_2) \)? Undecidable: Equivalence of two CFGs (whether they generate the same language) is an undecidable problem. \( L(G_1) \cap L(G_2) = \emptyset \)? Undecidable: The problem of checking whether two CFGs generate disjoint languages is undecidable. \( L(G_1) = L(R) \)? Undecidable: Checking whether a CFG generates the same language as a regular expression is undecidable. \( L(G_1) = \emptyset \)? Decidable: The emptiness problem for CFGs is decidable (Checking whether there exists a derivation from the start symbol leading to a terminal string). \hline
\end{array}
\]

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

  1. (i) - (a), (ii) - (b), and (iii) - (c)
  2. (i) - (b), (ii) - (a), and (iii) - (c)
  3. (i) - (b), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (a)
  4. (i) - (a), (ii) - (c), and (iii) - (b)
questions.explanation: CFL languages are closed under all operations except complement, intersection, and difference.  Recursive languages are not closed under substitution and homomorphism.  Regular languages are closed under all operations. So option $(B, C)$ is correct. for more:  Closure Property of Language Families

questions.explanation: Given that L accepted by a non-deterministic finite automata with 'n' states. Option A: L may have an accepting NFA with < n states. questions.questionText: Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers. $$\begin{aligned} L_{1} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{m} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \\ L_{2} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{n} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \end{aligned}$$ Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT? Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are context-free languages. $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language. $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers.

$$\begin{aligned} L_{1} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{m} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \\ L_{2} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{n} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \end{aligned}$$

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.
  2. $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language.
  3. $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language.
  4. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.

options.label: B
options.text: $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language.

options.label: C
options.text: $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language.

questions.explanation: Given: $L1=\{  a^m b^m c^{m+n}  ∣  m,n≥1  \}$ We can write this as: $L1 = \{  a^m b^m c^m⋅c^n  ∣  m,n≥1 \} = \{ a^m b^m c^m c^+ \} $  $L1 =\{ a^m b^m c^m c^+ \}$ So this seems like: $a^m b^m c^m$ followed by at least one more $c$ The language ${ a^m b^m c^m }$ is not context-free .It is a classic example of a language that is not context-free , because if we push $a$ ,pop $b$ then there will be no element for $c$ to be compared. Now for  $L2 = \{a^m b^n c^{m+n} ∣ m,n≥1\}$ For this language we can push $a,b$ then pop $c.$ Therefore, L1 is not Context free but L2 is context free Answer : $C$ Tejaswee_Bommaluleni answered Jul 9, 2025 • edited Jan 17 by Umesh Shelke Tejaswee_Bommaluleni comment Share Follow See all 3 Comments 3 3 Comments reply msrsaditya commented Aug 9, 2025 reply Follow flag if there's a^nb^nc^2n then it's not CFL because we're not checking # a's and # b's but if there's a^mb^nc^m+n t

questions.questionText: Consider the context-free grammar $G$ below \[ \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a S b \mid X \\ X \rightarrow a X \mid X b \mid a \mid b, \end{array} \] where $S$ and $X$ are non-terminals, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is $S$. Which one of the following statements is $\text{CORRECT}?$ The language generated by $G$ is $(a+b)^{\ast}$ The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$ The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$ The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the context-free grammar $G$ below
\[
\begin{array}{l}
S \rightarrow a S b \mid X \\
X \rightarrow a X \mid X b \mid a \mid b,
\end{array}
\]
where $S$ and $X$ are non-terminals, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is $S$.

Which one of the following statements is $\text{CORRECT}?$

  1. The language generated by $G$ is $(a+b)^{\ast}$
  2. The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$
  3. The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$
  4. The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language

options.label: B
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast}(a+b) b^{\ast}$

options.label: C
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is $a^{\ast} b^{\ast}(a+b)$

options.label: D
options.text: The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language

questions.explanation: Given productions of grammar G : S → aSb / X   X → aX / Xb / a / b    NOTE : While finding the expression for any given Grammar G, always try to solve in bottom up fashion.    For X : In X, any number of a & b can occur and when we wish to terminate, we have choice between a & b.   So, X → $a^{m}(a+b) / (a+b)b^{p}$ $(m \geq 0, p \geq 0)$   Replace this X in above productions. Then productions will look like this : S → aSb / $a^{m}(a+b) / (a+b)b^{p}$.   For S : Let’s first analyze S → aSb S → aSb S → aaSbb S → aaaSbbb    This is simply, $a^{n}b^{n}$ ($n\geq 1$). Let’s Substitute this :   S → $a^{n}a^{m}(a+b)b^{n} / a^{n}(a+b)b^{p}b^{n}$   This can further be simplified as :  $a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$ Option B , is correct answer.

questions.questionText: Consider the pushdown automaton $\text{(PDA)}\;P$ below, which runs on the input alphabet $\{a, b\}$, has stack alphabet $\{\perp, A\}$, and has three states $\{s, p, q\}$, with $s$ being the start state. A transition from state $u$ to state $v$, labelled $c / X / \gamma$, where $c$ is an input symbol or $\epsilon, X$ is a stack symbol, and $\gamma$ is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state $u$, the $\text{(PDA)}$ can read $c$ from the input, with $X$ on the top of its stack, pop $X$ from the stack, push in the string $\gamma$ on the stack, and go to state $v$. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol $\perp$ in it. The $\text{(PDA)}$ accepts by empty stack. Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by $P ?$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 1 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.n \lt m\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n \leq m\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.0 \leq n\right\}$ $\left\{a^{m} \mid 0 \leq m\right\} \cup\left\{b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n\right\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the pushdown automaton $\text{(PDA)}\;P$ below, which runs on the input alphabet $\{a, b\}$, has stack alphabet $\{\perp, A\}$, and has three states $\{s, p, q\}$, with $s$ being the start state. A transition from state $u$ to state $v$, labelled $c / X / \gamma$, where $c$ is an input symbol or $\epsilon, X$ is a stack symbol, and $\gamma$ is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state $u$, the $\text{(PDA)}$ can read $c$ from the input, with $X$ on the top of its stack, pop $X$ from the stack, push in the string $\gamma$ on the stack, and go to state $v$. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol $\perp$ in it. The $\text{(PDA)}$ accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by $P ?$

  1. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 1 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.n \lt m\right\}$
  2. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n \leq m\right\}$
  3. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid 0 \leq m\right.$ and $\left.0 \leq n\right\}$
  4. $\left\{a^{m} \mid 0 \leq m\right\} \cup\left\{b^{n} \mid 0 \leq n\right\}$

Empty String $\epsilon$ is Not accepted because from initial state, on empty tape, we cannot empty our stack since stack bottom symbol $\bot$ can be removed only in state $q$ But on empty tape, we can not reach to state $q$ from state $s.$ Method 2: Note that to empty our stack, the stack bottom symbol $\bot$ can be removed only in state $q.$ To reach state $q$, from $s$ or from $p,$ we need symbol $A$ on Top-of-the-stack (TOS). Symbol $A$ is pushed in the stack by symbol $a$ in the input string. questions.questionText: Suppose we want to design a synchronous circuit that processes a string of $0$’s and $1$’s. Given a string, it produces another string by replacing the first $1$ in any subsequence of consecutive $1$’s by a $0$. Consider the following example. $$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Input sequence:} &  00100011000011100 \\ \text{Output sequence:} & 00000001000001100 \end{array}$$ A  Mealy Machine  is a state machine where both the next state and the output are functions of the present state and the current input. The above mentioned circuit can be designed as a two-state Mealy machine. The states in the Mealy machine can be represented using Boolean values $0$ and $1$. We denote the current state, the next state, the next incoming bit, and the output bit of the Mealy machine by the variables $s, t, b$ and $y$ respectively. Assume the initial state of the Mealy machine is $0$. What are the Boolean expressions corresponding to $t$ and $y$ in terms of $s$ and $b$? $\begin{array}{l} t=s+b \\ y=sb \end{array}$ $\begin{array}{l} t=b \\ y=sb \end{array}$ $\begin{array}{l} t=b \\ y=s \overline{b} \end{array}$ $\begin{array}{l} t=s+b \\ y=s \overline{b} \end{array}$

A Mealy Machine is a state machine where both the next state and the output are functions of the present state and the current input.

The above mentioned circuit can be designed as a two-state Mealy machine. The states in the Mealy machine can be represented using Boolean values $0$ and $1$. Assume the initial state of the Mealy machine is $0$.

What are the Boolean expressions corresponding to $t$ and $y$ in terms of $s$ and $b$?

  3. $\begin{array}{l} t=b \\ y=s \overline{b} \end{array}$
