Neither $L_1$ nor $L_2$ is context- free. $L_1$ context- free but  $L_2$ is not context-free.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following languages.

$$\begin{array}{ll} L_1= \{ wxyx \mid w,x,y \in (0+1)^{+} \} \\ L_2= \{xy \mid x,y \in (a+b)^{*}, \mid x \mid=\mid y \mid, x \neq y \} \end{array}$$

Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. $L_1$ is regular and $L_2$ is context- free.
  2. $L_1$ context- free but not regular and $L_2$ is context-free.
  3. Neither $L_1$ nor $L_2$ is context- free.
  4. $L_1$ context- free but  $L_2$ is not context-free.

options.label: A
options.text: $L_1$ is regular and $L_2$ is context- free.

options.label: B
options.text: $L_1$ context- free but not regular and $L_2$ is context-free.

options.label: D
options.text: $L_1$ context- free but $L_2$ is not context-free.

questions.excerpt: A dice is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum of outcomes is a prime number?$3 / 36$ $19 / 36$ $15 / 36$ $13 / 36$
questions.questionText: A dice is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum of outcomes is a prime number? $3 / 36$ $19 / 36$ $15 / 36$ $13 / 36$
questions.questionHtml:
A dice is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum of outcomes is a prime number?

  1. $3 / 36$
     
  2. $19 / 36$
     
  3. $15 / 36$
     
  4. $13 / 36$
questions.explanation: 1. Find the Total Number of Outcomes A standard die has 6 faces {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} When a die is thrown twice, the total number of possible outcomes is: {Total Outcomes} = 6 * 6 = 36 2. Identify Possible Prime Sums The minimum sum possible is 1 + 1 = 2 The maximum sum possible is 6 + 6 = 12. The prime numbers between 2 and 12 are: 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 . 3. Count the Favorable Outcomes Now, we list the pairs (x, y) from each throw that add up to these prime numbers: Sum = 2: (1, 1) — 1 outcome Sum = 3: (1, 2), (2, 1)$ — 2 outcomes Sum = 5: (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)$ — 4 outcomes Sum = 7: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1) — 6 outcomes Sum = 11: (5, 6), (6, 5) — 2 outcomes Total Favorable Outcomes  = 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15$ 4. Calculate the Probability The probability (P) is the ratio of favorable outcomes to the total number of outcomes: P = \frac{\text{Favorable Outcomes}}/{{Total Outcomes}} P = 15/36 akash_kumar 9 answered Feb 13 akash_kumar 9 comm

questions.questionHtml:
A day can be either cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is $0.5$, independent of the condition of other days, then find the probability for any given $4$ days such that it will be $3$ cloudy days and $1$ sunny day.

  1. $1 / 4$
     
  2. $2 / 3$
     
  3. $3 / 4$
     
  4. $3 / 8$
questions.explanation: Each day can be Cloudy (C) or Sunny (S) with probability 0.5, and days are independent. Total days = 4 P(Cloudy) = 0.5 P(Sunny) = 0.5 We need the probability of exactly 3 cloudy days and 1 sunny day. Number of ways to choose 3 cloudy days out of 4: 4C3 = 4 Probability of any one specific arrangement (e.g., CCCS): (0.5)^3 × (0.5)^1 = (0.5)^4 = 1/16 Since there are 4 such arrangements, Required probability = 4 × (1/16) = 4/16 = 1/4 Final Answer: 1/4 Mehakpreet_Singh 1 answered Feb 14 Mehakpreet_Singh 1 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Column-I has statements made by Shanthala; and, Column-II has responses given by Kanishk. \( \begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}     \hline      & \textbf{Column-I} &  & \textbf{Column-II} \\     \hline     \textbf{P.} &\text{This house is in a mess.} & \textbf{1.} & \text{Alright, I won’t bring it up during} \\&&& \text{our conversations.} \\     \hline     \textbf{Q.} &\text{I am not happy with the marks} \\& \text{given to me.} & \textbf{2.} &\text{Well, you can easily look it up.} \\     \hline     \textbf{R.} &\text{Politics is a subject I avoid talking}\\& \text{about.} & \textbf{3.} &\text{No problem, let me clear it up for}\\&&& \text{you.} \\     \hline     \textbf{S.} &\text{I don’t know what this word}\\& \text{means.} & \textbf{4.} &\text{Don’t worry, I will take it up with}\\&&& \text{your teacher.} \\     \hline \end{array} \) Identify the option that has the correct match between Column-I and Column-II. $\mathrm{P}-2 ; \mathrm{Q}-3 ; \mathrm{R}-1 ; \mathrm{S}-4$ $\mathrm{P}-3 ; \mathrm{Q}-4 ; \mathrm{R}-1 ; \mathrm{S}-2$ $\mathrm{P}-4 ; \mathrm{Q}-1 ; \mathrm{R}-2 ; \mathrm{S}-3$ $\mathrm{P}-1 ; \mathrm{Q}-2 ; \mathrm{R}-4 ; \mathrm{S}-3$
questions.questionHtml:
Column-I has statements made by Shanthala; and, Column-II has responses given by Kanishk.

\(
\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}
    \hline
     & \textbf{Column-I} &  & \textbf{Column-II} \\
    \hline
    \textbf{P.} &\text{This house is in a mess.} & \textbf{1.} & \text{Alright, I won’t bring it up during} \\&&& \text{our conversations.} \\
    \hline
    \textbf{Q.} &\text{I am not happy with the marks} \\& \text{given to me.} & \textbf{2.} &\text{Well, you can easily look it up.} \\

    \hline
\end{array}
\)

questions.questionText: Moving into a world of big data will require us to change our thinking about the merits of exactitude. To apply the conventional mindset of measurement to the digital, connected world of the twenty-first century is to miss a crucial point. As mentioned earlier, the obsession with exactness is an artefact of the information-deprived analog era. When data was sparse, every data point was critical, and thus great care was taken to avoid letting any point bias the analysis. From “BIG DATA” Viktor Mayer-Schonberger and Kenneth Cukier. The main point of the paragraph is: The twenty-first century is a digital world Big data is obsessed with exactness Exactitude is not critical in dealing with big data Sparse data leads to a bias in the analysis
questions.questionHtml:
Moving into a world of big data will require us to change our thinking about the merits of exactitude. To apply the conventional mindset of measurement to the digital, connected world of the twenty-first century is to miss a crucial point. As mentioned earlier, the obsession with exactness is an artefact of the information-deprived analog era. When data was sparse, every data point was critical, and thus great care was taken to avoid letting any point bias the analysis. From “BIG DATA” Viktor Mayer-Schonberger and Kenneth Cukier. The main point of the paragraph is:

  1. The twenty-first century is a digital world
  2. Big data is obsessed with exactness
  3. Exactitude is not critical in dealing with big data
  4. Sparse data leads to a bias in the analysis
